title: Pitch Becomes a Place Along the Cochlea

scenes.tts: One kind of cell, the hair cell, tells you that a violin is playing an A. A hair cell turns a tiny movement into a graded voltage. But how does a coiled tube turn pitch into something a cell can read? Uncoil the cochlea, and the answer runs along its length. Frequency is turned into position.
scenes.visual: A violin A and a hair cell point at a question mark on a coiled tube; the coil unrolls into a strip, base left and apex right, and frequency becomes position.
scenes.narration: One kind of cell, the hair cell, tells you that a violin is playing an A. A hair cell turns a tiny movement into a graded voltage. But how does a coiled tube turn pitch into something a cell can read? Uncoil the cochlea, and the answer runs along its length. Frequency is turned into position.

scenes.tts: Cochlear hair cells sit on the basilar membrane, which runs the length of the coil. Near the base, where sound enters, the membrane is narrow and stiff. Toward the apex it is wider and more compliant. So the membrane has a stiffness gradient from base to apex.
scenes.visual: Hair cells appear on the strip; sound arrows enter at the base; the strip is narrow and stiff at the base, wide and compliant at the apex, with a stiffness gradient bar.
scenes.narration: Cochlear hair cells sit on the basilar membrane, which runs the length of the coil. Near the base, where sound enters, the membrane is narrow and stiff. Toward the apex it is wider and more compliant. So the membrane has a stiffness gradient from base to apex.

scenes.tts: Sound entering at the base sets up a travelling wave. It moves from base to apex, and grows until it reaches the place whose stiffness suits its frequency. There it peaks, and then it dies away. High frequencies peak near the base. Low frequencies peak near the apex.
scenes.visual: A sketched wave runs along the strip, grows, peaks and dies; a high tone peaks near the base, then a low tone near the apex.
scenes.narration: Sound entering at the base sets up a travelling wave. It moves from base to apex, and grows until it reaches the place whose stiffness suits its frequency. There it peaks, and then it dies away. High frequencies peak near the base. Low frequencies peak near the apex.

scenes.tts: Greenwood's function gives the place of each frequency in the human cochlea. Assume a cochlea thirty five millimetres long. A tone of one thousand hertz peaks fourteen millimetres from the apex, which is twenty one millimetres from the base. A tone of four thousand hertz peaks eleven point seven millimetres from the base, nearer than the lower tone. These two tones, two octaves apart, sit nine point three millimetres apart.
scenes.caption: Greenwood's function gives the place of each frequency in the human cochlea. Assume a cochlea 35 mm long. A tone of 1,000 Hz peaks 14.0 mm from the apex, which is 21.0 mm from the base. A tone of 4,000 Hz peaks 11.7 mm from the base, nearer than the lower tone. These two tones, two octaves apart, sit 9.3 mm apart.
scenes.visual: The 35 mm strip with a ruler; the worked arithmetic places the 1,000 Hz peak and the 4,000 Hz peak and a brace marks 9.3 mm between them.

scenes.tts: Von Békésy measured these waves, many of them in human cadaver cochleas. His peaks were far broader than the tuning of a living ear. The difference is an amplifier. Outer hair cells change length when their voltage changes, and on each cycle of a sound they push on the membrane in step. This adds energy at the peak, which sharpens tuning and raises sensitivity.
scenes.visual: A broad grey peak and a sharp living-ear outline; outer hair cells lengthen and shorten in step under the peak, and the broad peak becomes taller and sharper.

scenes.tts: This map of frequency onto position is called tonotopy. The auditory nerve ends in the cochlear nucleus, then come the superior olivary complex and the inferior colliculus. The medial geniculate nucleus then relays to auditory cortex. Keep this rule: frequency becomes position, kept as a coarse map through the main relays.
scenes.visual: A column of relays from auditory nerve to auditory cortex, each carrying the same low-to-high frequency bar.
